extracted.intended_audience: business writers and financial-advice/content authors considering hiring a sensitivity reader to improve diversity/inclusion in their work
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on hiring and working with a sensitivity reader for business or investment-related writing, including how to choose a reader, expected process, fees, deliverables, and how to use their feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a sensitivity reader is useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with a sensitivity reader can be useful, especially if you don’t work with a community of people who can give you targeted feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sensitivity reader to expand perspective and get targeted feedback on diversity/inclusion issues when you lack an existing community or colleagues who can provide that input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match reader expertise to the identities/issues in your manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may be members of the groups the writers are discussing or targeting; pick someone with the relevant background (race, religion, disability, regional culture, family experience, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review reader profiles for characteristics and lived experience relevant to your manuscript (examples given: Chinese-American culture, Muslim/Arab/Egyptian, regional Southern upbringing, cerebral palsy, infertility/IVF, etc.). Sensitivity reading isn’t just for race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reader’s professional experience (e.g., corporate clients)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you might refer work or need a reader accustomed to corporate contexts, look for readers experienced working with corporate clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the service/contact to highlight readers experienced with corporate work; that informed the author's selection of a reader (Mya) who was available and had relevant experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and scheduling expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Service provided lists of readers who could start immediately and readers with longer wait times; site states 'All edits will take a minimum of 3 weeks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan timelines around minimum turnaround times and potential waitlists; confirm availability before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees, deposit, and contractual terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation of a 50% down-payment and signing a legal agreement (DocuSign). Salt & Sage charged a minimum and per-word rates (minimums changed from $65 to $140; quoted rate .009c/word), with flexible payment plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for upfront payment and a written contract. Confirm current minimums, per-word rates, any price changes, and payment options before sending manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service communication model (no direct contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: All communications go through Salt & Sage staff. You won’t have direct contact with your sensitivity reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the intermediary model: questions, clarifications, and scheduling are handled by staff rather than direct author-reader exchange; factor this into expectations for back-and-forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverables from a sensitivity read
rubrics_metrics.description: You will typically receive a marked-up copy of your document and a separate letter from the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect both inline edits/comments and a summarizing letter that explains perspectives, rationale, and recommended resources or links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and tone of reader feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers provide perspective, not gatekeeping: 'I am only one person with the perspective of one person. I am not a gatekeeper, nor do I have final say ... My goal is to shine a light on areas that might be improved and give you further resources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat feedback as advisory — a sensitivity reader offers observations and resources rather than mandates. Use their input to inform edits, not as absolute rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical types of sensitivity feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include suggesting elaboration on why word choice is important, providing links to resources, and recommending alternative phrasing (e.g., discussion that 'people with a disability' isn’t always preferred to 'the disabled'; capitalization issues like 'white' vs 'White').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect attention to word choice, terminology, cultural context, and references; readers may suggest external resources to justify recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer discretion in adopting suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author incorporated some suggestions (links, phrasing) but declined others where content already covered or for editorial reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may accept some recommendations and decline others depending on context, prior content, or editorial constraints; document reasons when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-saving or alternative options (Incomplete Guides)
rubrics_metrics.description: For clients with smaller budgets, the service offers 'Incomplete Guides' giving overviews of several identities (e.g., Writing Queer Characters, Writing Nonbinary Characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lower-cost guide products or summaries if a full sensitivity read is beyond your budget or you need general orientation rather than manuscript-level feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral/discount incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: You can get a 10% discount by using the author’s name; services may have referral discounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about discounts or referral codes before purchase to reduce cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect legal/administrative paperwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Author had to sign a 'surprisingly long legal agreement' via DocuSign before work began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and be aware of contract terms (usage rights, confidentiality, liability, cancellation, etc.) and retain copies for your records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity readers as part of a broader 'village' of resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The author credited multiple sources (writer communities, editors attuned to racial issues, DEI initiatives, local training programs) for improving work on sensitive topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sensitivity reader input with community feedback, editorial colleagues, DEI initiatives and training to form a more robust review process.
